note: Aesthetic axes for world authoring. The axes are fixed by the world schema: every concept carries the same five system rules, so these read those rules rather than inventing a parallel vocabulary. Only the values are authored, and they exist to be drawn from before a design is made, because a generator left to choose its own aesthetic picks the safe one every time; that is the same anti-argmax mechanism the concept seeder uses on candidate order. Occupancy is measured against the approved corpus and the draw is weighted inversely to it, so the catalog acts as an exclusion map rather than a template. Axes marked recorded cannot be probed from prose at all and are only exact once a wave assigns and records them on the concept. Two probe kinds: a keyword axis asks whether a rule says a thing, a count axis asks how many things it names. Prefer counting where the rules enumerate rather than characterise, which is why chroma counts pigments. An axis that places less than 60% of the corpus reports itself unreliable and is excluded from the ranked openings, because a value nobody matches looks exactly like an opening and is not one.

axes.label: Palette breadth
axes.question: How many colours does the palette name?
axes.note: Counted, not keyword-matched. Palette rules enumerate pigments (lapis and vermilion over cream) rather than naming a strategy, so probing for 'monochrome' or 'full spectrum' placed 9 of 281 worlds. Counting the colours a rule names places 93% and shows the real shape: the corpus clusters hard at three or four.

axes.label: Colour strategy
axes.question: How much of the surface does colour occupy?
axes.note: The skill's own vocabulary, from reference/new-work.md, so a world authored against it speaks the language the build phase already uses. Distinct from chroma: chroma counts how many colours a palette names, this says how much surface they cover. A two-colour drenched world and a two-colour restrained world are opposite designs. Places only 7% of the corpus, which is a finding rather than a broken probe: these worlds were authored before the vocabulary was applied to them. State it explicitly when authoring rather than widening these keywords.

values.label: full palette: three or four named roles
drenched: the surface is the colour

axes.label: Surface material
axes.question: What is the surface made of?

axes.label: Spatial metaphor
axes.question: What kind of space is this, physically?
axes.note: Replaces the depth axis, which measured almost nothing and was derived from material anyway. Reads the topology rule the schema already has, and covers the same intuition with far more range: a sheet and a machine are different spaces before they are different surfaces. Values rebuilt from the nouns and movement verbs the topology rules actually use, rather than guessed.

axes.label: Density
axes.question: How much lives on one screen, and is emptiness luxury or waste?
axes.note: Proposed independently by all three reviews with near-identical values, and argued by each to be the strongest single predictor of not reading as generated. Values rebuilt from the density words the corpus actually uses (open, margin, dense, tight, packed). A first attempt matched the bare word 'every', which appears in 129 worlds ('every entry point', 'every meaningful state') and pushed the axis over the trust threshold on its own. An axis can be trusted for the wrong reason, so a value carrying a common English word is worse than no value.

values.label: saturated: every part of the ground worked

axes.label: Compositional law
axes.question: What law places things on the page?
axes.note: Type/composition currently bundles placement into one prose sentence, so a generator resolves it as centred hero every time. Enumerating it removes the default. Mueller-Brockmann against Ed Fella. Values rebuilt from the placement vocabulary the composition rules actually use.

axes.label: Scale dynamic range
axes.question: How far apart are the largest and smallest elements?
axes.note: Rules name the poles rather than a ratio: display, headline, caption, small. Values read those, so this measures whether a world states a scale contrast at all and roughly how wide. A ratio would be exact and is worth recording when a wave assigns one.

values.label: narrow: one size does most of the work

axes.label: Motion law
axes.question: How does the design move, and under what law? (Under-authored: see note.)
axes.note: Not mis-probed: the corpus does not author motion. Only 28% of Responsive/motion rules mention any motion verb, while 58% describe responsive adaptation and the rest accessibility. That rule is doing reflow-and-access duty, so motion law is effectively unauthored. The fix is to state it explicitly when authoring, not to widen these keywords.

axes.label: Prohibition
axes.question: What does this world refuse to do?
axes.note: The one axis that subtracts. Every other axis grants a property, so an agent can satisfy the whole grid by adding one more nice thing; a refusal cannot be satisfied that way. Drawn for every world, because a world with no refusal has no edges. Grounded in Irma Boom's Chanel No 5 book, printed entirely blind-embossed with no ink, and Barnbrook's Blackstar, black on black. Recorded only: an absence cannot be probed for in prose.

values.label: no more than one type size
no ink on the ground plane

axes.label: Variance law
axes.question: What may differ between two applications of this identity, and what drives the difference?
axes.note: The largest measured hole: 0 to 1% of the corpus describes variance at all. An identity is a contract about what stays fixed and what is allowed to change, which is what separates Tate and the Whitney from a style. Chosen over input primacy and temporality because every register can answer it, where a landing page has no input primacy and a docs page is always a snapshot. Recorded only: it cannot be seen in one instance.

values.label: parametric: fixed skeleton, one dimension stretches
curated chaos: each instance redrawn, coherence carried by voice

incompatible.reason: Ink absorbed into stock cannot also be a lit surface. One is reflective, the other emits.
A world that refuses ink on the ground plane cannot be made of printed ink on stock.
One type size cannot also be an extreme scale range; the refusal forecloses the axis.
A refusal of rules, dividers and boxes cannot coexist with a rational modular grid whose bands and registers are drawn.
An immutable identity cannot have form computed from data; generative is variance by definition.

incompatibleNote: Declared contradictions only, deliberately short. These exist because an empty cell in a correlated pair is often empty because the combination cannot exist rather than because nobody tried it, and weighting a draw toward it sends a wave after nonsense. A long invented matrix would do the opposite harm, quietly shrinking the space it claims to protect, so add a pair only when you can state why it cannot exist.
